source_text: Rectius enim accipit nomen mali quam boni, unde erubescunt mali et boni, meliusque credimus Apostolo, qui dicit: " Quia non habitat in carne mea bonum " [n190] , quam huic, qui hoc dicit bonum.
pass_a_gloss: For it more rightly takes the name of evil than of good, whence both evils and goods blush, and we believe better the Apostle, who says: Because good does not dwell in my flesh, than this one who says this is good.

lemmas.lexica: LS bonum; Blaise good-of-nature vs good-of-will
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: [Augustine continues:] ‘For what makes both evil and good people blush is more rightly called evil than good. We do better to believe the apostle, who says, “Good does not dwell in my flesh” (Romans 7:18), than this man who calls it good.’

choices.why: Paul in Julian's citations; keep Apostle not 'Paul' unless Paulus is written.
Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
